utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the Registrar call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, Stevan Todorovic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, we are to begin today's proceedings with evidence from Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There are just two or three minor matters that I would like to bring out before calling my first witness. The first matter, Your Honour: I take it from the comments made by Judge Hunt with regard to the writ of habeas corpus petition, that it is not entertained by Chambers, will that only remain an oral decision or will that be followed by a written decision?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm afraid you can't verbal me quite like that, Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You can't verbal me quite like that. What I said was we have no power to make an order for a writ for habeas corpus. I said the issue has to be dealt with as an application to challenge the legality of your client's detention. Nobody said that your writ, so-called, will not be entertained, but not in the form in which it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, I think we have had enough of this. Let's not get diverted by classifications and nomenclature. My inclination is to deal with substance, not procedure. You have filed what you called a writ of habeas corpus. The Tribunal's Statute does not recognise a writ of habeas corpus. But essentially a writ of habeas corpus seeks to challenge the legality of the detention of an accused person, and we have an obligation to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. All I was asking for was a very simple clarification. My second point, Your Honour, is that with regard to my calling Mr. Todorovic as a witness, I would like to have a motion in limine whereby my client's right not to testify against him be still continued and that his testimony is for the purposes of whatever we want to call it, either a writ of habeas corpus or a motion testing his detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, we are hearing two motions, and ultimately the Chamber will give its decision on the two motions: the writ of habeas corpus, if you prefer that classification, or the challenge to the legality of the accused's detention; and secondly, the writ for the return of the accused. With regard to the in limine point, the accused may, of course, be cross-examined but not to the questions that go to his guilt or innocence. The cross-examination will be limited to the examination-in-chief and to the questions that are pertinent to this particular inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The last point is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you. I filed a motion with the Court early this morning, and I made an error stating September 27th and 28th. The dates in the motion should be 26th and 27th, and as soon as I get back to New York on Friday, I will refile a corrected version, but I did not want to have the Chamber be misled by my early-morning mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have only just received that motion and we haven't yet had a chance to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With regard -- that ends the preliminary matters, and the Todorovic Defence would then call Mr. Todorovic in support of the motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Neimann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My understanding of the proceedings today was to hear the motion in the nature of habeas corpus. It wasn't my understanding that there was going to be any motion -- hearing of the motion in relation to the return of the accused, and if that is to occur today, well, I object to that on the grounds that these issues have been well litigated on numerous occasions by previous motions that have been brought by the accused. My understanding of the exchange between us yesterday, Your Honours, was that a new matter had arisen, namely, the writ of habeas corpus or the proceedings in nature of that, and that was a matter where this accused had not, in the past, challenged the warrant or the validity of his arrest. That is one matter, and I acknowledge that that was, in effect, the case. I didn't believe it to be at the time, and I still don't believe it to be a matter of issue between the parties, but if he wishes to pursue it, I didn't raise objection. But, Your Honours, I certainly do object to going into the second issue, which in my submission has been canvassed extensively in numerous motions that have been brought and, in fact, it has gone as far as the Court of Appeal and back down again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, speaking for myself, I am not in agreement with that. We are, in fact, hearing two motions. They are to a certain extent linked, and for practical purposes it's convenient to hear them. The previous motion that you spoke of that went to the Court of Appeal was dismissed by this Chamber on the ground that there was not presented sufficient evidence. The Appeals Chamber held that this Chamber was correct in exercising that discretion and coming to that conclusion. The accused has subsequently presented evidence as to what he considers to be an illegality and it is that which is being canvassed today and that is a new matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If I may say so, not having been there myself but from reading all the material, the only issue which was determined in the previous proceedings was where the onus of proof lay, and that's the only matter that went to the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Wait a minute, Mr. Niemann. There's no finding that there's no consideration in any of the decisions to all of the submissions which the Prosecution has made as to what the law was. It was simply an issue that he had presented no evidence, he asserting that the Prosecution had the onus of proof, and the Prosecution correcting saying, "No, it's not our onus." Now, that was held against him. He's now come back accepting that he's led evidence, but no other issue was determined in any of those proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the procedure that he decided upon failed and he made, presumably, an intelligent assessment of the course that he would seek to pursue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think we debated this yesterday, Mr. Niemann, and I pointed out to you that the Appeals Chamber decision, to which you referred correctly, said that you are not debarred from bringing a second application if some new circumstance arises. Well, the new circumstance which arises is he's been proved wrong as to his contention as to where the onus of proof lay, and I asked you yesterday whether you were still pursuing the technicality that you were relying upon rather than the merits of the case. Now, I know that you did not concede anything, but it was made very clear to you yesterday that that was why we were going on to hear this second application.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My understanding, Your Honour, was that the discussion yesterday was related to the motion in the nature of habeas corpus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps you were in error, and you've made your bed to lie on, just as you are asserting that the applicant made his.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, in that event, Your Honours, I can only take it that Your Honours overrule my objection based on the fact that these matters have been previously litigated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Todorvic Defence calls Stevan Todorovic to the stand. May I inquire of the procedure, Your Honour, will the witness be testifying from the place in the dock, or will he be testifying from the witness chair?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He will be testifying from the witness chair. Let the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, are you the accused in this case?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And at one time, you lived at Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: In July of 1998, where were you residing?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In July of 1998, I was in Serbia, in the town of Rudine, in the municipality of Cajetina, at Mt. Zlatibor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... as the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: When did you move from Bosanski Samac to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In January 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: When you moved from Bosanski Samac to Yugoslavia, did you cross an international border?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did you use --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brashich, I need to interrupt you for a moment, just for the clarity of this testimony. You should ask -- I should like you to ask the witness, what was his nationality at the time -- that is, his citizenship -- at the time when he left Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: What was your nationality in January of 1998?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The citizenship was one of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did you have a passport or a personal identity card issued by the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I had a personal identification card of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And when was that identity document issued?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I believe in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And by whom?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: By the Ministry of the Interior of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And what document did you use when you went across the border between Republika Srpska and Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I used my personal identification card.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please be advised to pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: In July, August, and September --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, you are being asked by the interpreters to observe a pause between the answer and the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: In July, August, and September of 1998, were you employed?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: By whom were you employed?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I worked in Cajetina, in the MUP [translation error].

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: What was the name of the company that employed you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: This was a private company called Danica in Cajetina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And what was the business of this enterprise?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, there is a mistake in the transcript. His answer, "I worked in Cajetina, in the MUP," which means "Police." It is not that the witness said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, would you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I thank my brother Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It was the interpreter's mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I repeat again: By what enterprise were you employed in July, August, and September of 1998?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: A private company called Danica, in Cajetina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: In July, August, or September, were you employed by any organ or part of the Yugoslav government?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: What was the business of this enterprise?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The enterprise produced and sold protective clothing for workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And what was your position with the firm?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I was an outside salesman. I sold these products.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: In September of 1998, where were you physically living?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I lived in the village of Rudine, in the Cajetina municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Just to visualise this little village of Rudine, what is the nearest large town?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The nearest sizeable town is Uzice, which is about 20 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did you live in a flat, or did you live in a house?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I lived in a small wooden house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did you live alone, or did you live with someone else?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I lived alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did that little house have an address?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It had an address. It was Rudine, no number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: On September 26th, 1998, were you in the village of Rudine at approximately 8.00 or 9.00 p.m. of that day?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: At that time, what, if anything, first happened to you at that house?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I raise an objection on the basis of relevance. It seems to me that the events that occurred at this particular time in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia can hardly be relevant to the arrest, which is the subject of this application, which subsequently occurred in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at Tuzla. And so, in my submission, Your Honours, none of this evidence of what occurred up until the time of the arrest is relevant at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is the Defence's position that this is the initial step that takes the defendant from his residence in Rudine in Yugoslavia, at approximately 9.00 on the 26th of September, and ends up at Tuzla air force base some ten hours thereafter, when -- and then there's a question, because if -- as the evidence will show, the detention by SFOR occurred sometime prior to any possible time that the defendant was placed under arrest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are you going to argue that the Prosecution is somehow responsible by colluding with whoever it was who is alleged to have kidnapped your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I am not prepared to argue that the Prosecution was in collusion; I am prepared to argue that the SFOR forces were in collusion with individuals who had abducted, kidnapped, my client from the territory of Yugoslavia, breaching that state's sovereignty, crossing illegally an internationally recognised boundary, and then breaching the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina prior to delivery to the Prosecution and this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So you are going to argue, are you, that even though the Prosecution was not responsible for this, somehow it's relevant? Is that what you're going to argue?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I would think that my argument would focus on the idea that the SFOR forces were acting as agents of the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right, yes, and that they colluded with the people who are alleged to have kidnapped your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So it's going to be a factual issue that you want to establish?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, do you want to reply? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's only that unless the situation has changed since my friend filed his various motions in this matter, because in a motion that he filed on the 20th of October, 1999, on page 2 of that motion, he says, in the statement in support of the motion, that: "In relation to this day" -- that is, the 26th of September -- "four individuals unknown to me, by use of force and threats and bodily harm," et cetera, and then he goes on to say, "I never consented to the four unknown individuals." So I raise this because, having seen this, it seems to me that unless circumstances have changed, unless he can promise to produce some evidence to refute that position, he stated -- not only on this occasion, but on this and other occasions -- that he simply doesn't know who they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He also said yesterday that he wasn't restricting himself to what was in that affidavit, and he said he had two more witnesses to call. Now, we haven't seen statements and there's nothing in the papers, but I thought that he has agreed with me he is going to lead evidence from which he is going to invite us to draw those inferences. We haven't got a very good case laid out for us to consider at this stage, but, nevertheless, if he's says he's going to prove it, we've got to let him attempt to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour. If the position has changed since he's filed those motions, then certainly I would withdraw my objection on that basis, but I sincerely hope that we are not going to be subjected to all this evidence only to hear that the situation is precisely the same as it was some months ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann. The Chamber is satisfied as to the relevance of this evidence. Proceed, Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question. On September 26th, at your home in Rudine, at approximately 8.00 or 9.00 that evening, what, if anything, happened initially?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Sometime around 8.00 I fell asleep. I had been watching television. Sometime around 9.00 I heard knocks on my door, and instinctively I jumped up and I just started towards the door. I could hear the yells by neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Where was the banging coming from?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: From the other side of the door, directly the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did you open the door?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I tried to open the door, and there was an unknown man who came through the door with a handgun pointing at me, and then he hit me over the head and threw me on the bed. The house was three to four metres long.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... accompanied by anybody else.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after that, he was followed by another man and then I saw two additional men, so altogether four men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... did he continue to hold the pistol, the gun?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did he say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: He said, "Why are you hiding? Come on, let's go."

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: What did you say to him?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I said that it must be a mistake, that there is no reason, and he said, "Quit talking. Get up and let's go."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, could I find out in what language was the person speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Were they speaking Serbian or were they speaking another language?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: They spoke Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And what did you say to them?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, please come closer to his microphone.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I was told it was a mistake --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, you're being asked by the interpreters to come closer to the microphone, and I think you're not observing the pause between the answer and the question. You're beginning to speak when the interpretation is not concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: What did you say to them?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I said that it must be a mistake, that there was no reason for me to go with them, because I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: After that, was anything said by you or by them further on this topic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The second one, the one with the baseball bat in his hand, he said, "Come. Let's go. We can't waste time talking to you."

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Then the two of them grabbed me by my two arms and dragged me out of that little house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did you agree to go with them?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: After you left the house, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: After I left that little house, they pulled me into a passenger car.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion to see the licence plates of that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Was it at that time light or dark outside?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It was dark, but light was coming from the house because the door was open, and the car was only three or four metres away from that little house, so that one could see the car and the plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: The licence plate that you saw, was that an official plate or was it a civilian plate?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Civilian plate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: In Yugoslavia, what is the difference between an official plate and a civilian plate licence plate?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Civilian plates have a white background and characters and figures are black, and the police vehicles have white letters and figures against a blue background.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... automobile, where did the five of you sit?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Then we were pushed onto a back seat and two of them sat to the left and right of me and the other two sat in front.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did you enter the vehicle voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did the automobile start moving?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: In which direction?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In the direction of the Belgrade-Podgorica highway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: When you got to the Belgrade-Podgorica highway, what, if anything, happened at that point?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: They stopped the vehicle when they came to the first enlarged area.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel please wait for the interpreters to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, really. If you perhaps put your headphones around your ears you would hear when the translation has concluded, that they're running a long time behind you when you start your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Was anything said?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Was anything said at the time that the vehicle stopped at the Belgrade-Podgorica highway?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: What, if anything, was said?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The man who was sitting next to the driver told the driver to get off and change the plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did you see the change of licence plates?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Was your eyesight in any way restricted at that time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the rear part of the car, yes, it was restricted. I saw the driver got out, but I don't know what he was doing outside. He only got off and very quickly he was back and continued on the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: In which direction did the car then start moving?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: He started towards Uzice and Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And for what period of time did you drive along that highway?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: We rode along that highway for about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: During those 30 minutes, was there any conversation? Did you have any conversation with the four men?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it took a very short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: What did they say to you and what did you say to them?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: They said to me that they were taking me because I was owing some money to somebody and they were to collect that debt. I answered that I didn't owe any money to anyone and that, therefore, there must have been some mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: When they first entered your home, did they show you any identification or badges?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did they show you any arrest warrant or court order for your detention?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: What happened thereafter? We're back on the road towards Uzice. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: They turned off that highway to the left, in the direction of Arilja Valjevo and the River Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: And after awhile, on an elevation where there were no houses or vehicles, they stopped the passenger car and told me that they were doing it for money and that they had been offered 20.000 German Marks. So if I had 40.000 to give them, they would set me free. As they were saying this, they tied my hands with a rope, and over that rope they put an adhesive tape, brown, three centimetres wide. On that same occasion they also blindfolded me with that same tape. I said -- I mean, where on earth could I find those 40.000 German Marks in cash? They said, "Well, try to remember somebody with a telephone," and they would talk to him over the mobile telephone, and if that person brought the money, that they would then set me free.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did anyone come to your mind that you could call?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No, not at first, but then I remembered that perhaps my cousin, my aunt's son, could perhaps find that money, so that later on I told them that perhaps they could call him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And this cousin of yours, where was he living or physically located?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: He lived in the village of Zlatina, near Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Stevo Tosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did you give these four men his name and telephone number?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: After you had given them his name, what, if anything, happened?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat the question. After you gave the name and the telephone number, did anybody call him?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Who made the call?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: One of those four. I believe it was the co-driver, the one who was sitting in front. I think it was he. Then he gave me the -- he handed me over the telephone and held me, because my hands were tied, to bring the telephone to my ear and resume the conversation with Tosic. I mean, they dialled the number and I heard them say, "Hello. Good evening. Is that Tosic? Your relative Stevan wants to talk to you."

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: What did you say to Mr. Tosic and what did he say to you during that conversation?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I told him that I had been kidnapped and that people who kidnapped me wanted 40.000 German Marks as ransom. He said, "Where do you want me to find 40.000 marks overnight? Nobody has all that cash." I told him that if he wanted to see me alive again, to try to do that, to borrow those 40.000 from someone and then try to bring them during the night or, rather, until 10.00 the next morning to bring it, because that's what they said, that he should bring those 40.000 marks to a petrol station near Belgrade by 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: After the end of that conversation, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: When I finished my conversation with Tosic, they told him, "Well, do as Stevan as told you, and we won't call you again. We'll see you tomorrow at 10.00." That is, that I would see him then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: And then we resumed the ride. After awhile they stopped the vehicle and two of those four got off that car; that is, only two stayed in the car with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Could you, at that time, see the direction in which you were travelling?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Approximately how much time passed from the initial pounding on the door until this point?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Two and a half, three hours, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did you ever consent to be held by these first four, then two men, during these two and a half to three hours?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: After the two men left, did you stay in the car?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: After the two men left, did the car move?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the vehicle resumed the journey, but we stopped frequently, and when changing the direction. And I also noticed they stopped at some place, and I felt a very unpleasant odour, and they also commented, said that it must be a garbage dump nearby, and I heard the loud music from a restaurant. And we moved away from that place and came back to it several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: For how long did you so drive?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: For another hour, or maybe one and a half or two, after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, during this time, is he still blindfolded? I just would like to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Would you describe your ability to move or to see during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I had this opaque tape over my eyes. To my left, one individual was sitting to my left, and after the two of those left, the back of the front seat was lowered down. And in front, at the wheel, was the one who was driving the vehicle. I could hear them talk now and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't see, nor I couldn't move. I couldn't get off, because I was blocked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, the last question was completely lost because you were speaking over the interpretation. What was it? I think it was probably "Did you see anything?"; the answer was, "No, I couldn't see." But do you remember what your question was?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: "Did you" -- "Were you able to see?" Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please wait until the translation is over.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: When did you exit the car?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I got out of the car when they stopped it, told me -- that is, got me by the -- by the hand and pulled me out of the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Once you exited the automobile, where did you go, and how did you get there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Two men got me by my two hands, and they dragged me over a concrete or an asphalt pavement, and then I felt that we were moving down a slope of some 20 to 30 metres long.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: You mentioned gravel. Can you be more specific as to the type of gravel?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, gravel; those were stones, pebbles, shingle that you find on the bank of a river or on the seacoast; that kind of shingle or pebbles. And I could also feel the smell of the river, the smell of the stale water, I mean the smell -- the kind that you feel when you come close to a river.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And what happened next? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: After that, they ordered me to sit down, and one held me whilst the other one was getting the boat ready. I could hear twigs cracking, and some other -- and branches, and then they pulled me onto a small boat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: At that time, were you free to move around and about?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't move about, because my hands were tied; I was blindfolded. And while they were preparing the boat, they also used that tape to immobilise my arms and my legs and all over my body.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did you voluntarily get into that boat?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did the boat move?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: How was the boat propelled?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It did not have an engine, so they rowed. Very quietly, so as not to be overheard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And how long were you in that boat?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was about 15 to 20 minutes in that boat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did the boat reach land?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Once the boat reached land, what happened?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: When the boat landed, they pulled me out of the boat and loaded me into the boot of a passenger vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did the vehicle move?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It did. I could hear the sound of the engine when they switched it on, and so we rode for a while up a slope and along a very winding route.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did the automobile come to a stop?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, after 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Once the automobile came to a stop, what happened?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The engine was switched off, or rather the car stopped, and I heard the sound of a manual radio, and then I heard a conversation in English which I couldn't follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: When you speak of a -- "manual radio" is the translation in the transcript -- what do you mean? What kind of manual radio?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It was a hand-held, the radio device that the police usually use, and we also used them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: So you were familiar with this particular radio device?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Why, yes, because it was a sound similar to the one produced by a radio device.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And the language spoken was English?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Do you speak or understand English?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after that, I heard the sound of a helicopter blade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, just let me be clear. The language spoken was English; that's the language coming from the radio as well as the language spoken by the persons who were holding him?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: When you were in the trunk of the car, and when the radio was used, could you hear both the person using the radio close to you as well as the person to whom he was speaking?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could hear directly both the persons who were talking into the radio and the responses which were coming to them through the radio speakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: The individual who was speaking next to the car, in what language was he speaking?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And the receiving language that you could hear was in what language?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Also English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Now, you heard the helicopter blades --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just one more question, Mr. Brashich. I'd like to find out, how long did that conversation last?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, how long did the radio transmission, the two-way radio transmission, take?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Very briefly. Several minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did a helicopter arrive on the scene?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: You could not see at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I could not see, but I could hear the sound. It was very loud.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: What happened after the helicopter landed?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: They opened the trunk, took me out of the trunk, and led me for some 50 metres over a bumpy, grassy terrain to the helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did you get in the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: They loaded me onto the helicopter. I did not walk on to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did you voluntarily go into that helicopter?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: From the time you left the riverbank to the time that the helicopter got there, did you voluntarily stay in the trunk of the car?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: From the time that you got to the riverbank to the time that the helicopter arrived, did anybody show you any identification?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: From the time that you got to the riverbank to the time the helicopter arrived, did anybody show you a warrant of arrest or a court order?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Once you got -- well, you were put into the helicopter. Did anyone say anything to you in the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did anyone identify themselves during the helicopter ride?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Were you shown, during your helicopter ride, any warrant of arrest or court order?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: How long was your helicopter ride?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: About 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Once the helicopter landed, what happened?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I was taken off the helicopter and taken across some concrete asphalt surface, and I was brought into a wooden structure, a prefabricated structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: At that point, when you entered that structure, were you able to see?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Then my blindfold was taken off, and then they cut the ties and the tape that my body was bandaged with and I was put in plastic handcuffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And there were people about you; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And could you describe these individuals?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The first men whom I saw were wearing SFOR uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Was anything said to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Mr. Brashich, could you ask the witness how did he know that it was SFOR uniforms and that those were SFOR uniforms? How did he know?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: At any time before September 26, 1998, did you have an occasion to see SFOR uniforms?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: On how many occasions?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: On several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: So by September 26th, 1998, you were familiar with the SFOR uniforms?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Was anything said to you at the time that they cut the rope, took off the tape, and put plastic handcuffs on you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was told that I was in the SFOR base in Tuzla. They asked me whether I wanted to drink some coffee. I declined. I had a drink of water and then I was given a document to sign, and beforehand an interpreter told me that -- said that anything I could say could be used against me, and following that I signed the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: At that time, were you being audio and videotaped?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, could you find out what document he signed?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: You have just testified as to a document. Was that document in the English or the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: This document was both in English and Serbian languages, and the text of the document was that from here on, anything I would say could be used against me and that I thereby acknowledge that this information was given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Was any other document given to you at that particular time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Approximately what time in the morning did you arrive at the Tuzla air force base?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: About 2.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: What happened thereafter?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: After that, the commander came. He was introduced to me as General Sinseki [phoen]. My handcuffs came off and he sat me down across from him and talked to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Approximately what time of the morning was that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: That was around 5.00, 5.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Could you tell us what General Sinseki [phoen] said to you and what you said to him at that 5.00 a.m. meeting?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: He asked me whether I knew how I arrived in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I briefly said that four unknown men had kidnapped me from Mount Zlatibor. He asked me what Zlatibor was. I told him that it was a tourist destination in Serbia, and that four unknown persons had kidnapped me, that they asked money of a cousin of mine. And then calling upon his officer's honour, I said -- since I was here -- whether he could call my cousin and tell him not to go there in order not to risk anything further and not to undergo any further stress. And the General asked me what the telephone number was, and I gave him the phone number, and he said that he may call him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: How long did this conversation take -- how long was this conversation?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: This conversation lasted about ten minutes. The General also asked me what they should do in order to catch Blagoje Simic, and I told him that I didn't know what they were supposed to do in order to get him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And Blagoje Simic is another defendant in this case?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And he is the gentleman that has not been arrested as of yet; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did General Sinseki [phoen] exhibit any papers to you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: What happened after he left?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: After he left, a doctor appeared and he conducted a detailed examination, which was also taped on camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Was the interview with the General taped?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: After the doctor examined you -- by the way, were you in any way hurt?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had a head injury. I had a laceration and I had some blood in my hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Who did that to you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I sustained this injury in the boat, when I was put in a boat. I felt a powerful blow and for a moment I lost consciousness, and I felt something wet and I felt hot -- something wet and warm on my face and my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: After the doctor left, who was the next person that you saw after the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Withdraw the question. Very cumbersome, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: After the doctor left, did you meet any other individual with regard to your detention?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The interpreter told me that this was an officer of The Hague Tribunal, from the Prosecutor's Office of The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Approximately what time in the morning was that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: This was sometime between 10.00 and 11.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Can you describe him for us?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It was a man, 40 to 45 years, with light brown hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Was this meeting with the representative of the ICTY audio and videotaped?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: What did this representative say to you and what did you say to him?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: He told me that the ICTY had issued an indictment against me, that they had a warrant for my arrest, and that I would be transported to The Hague by plane.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Were you transported -- withdrawn. Did he exhibit any documents to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: What did he exhibit?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. There were some photographs there and there were several different documents, including the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Did you travel to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in the afternoon. We left around 1.00 or 2.00, and I arrived in The Hague in the early hours of the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: When you got to The Hague, where were you lodged?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I was placed in the U.N. detention unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And are you still there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brashich, I have yet another question which I should like the witness to answer. I believe that he said that he had left Bosanski Samac in July 1998, and I should like you to ask the witness why did he decide to leave Bosanski Samac and move over to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, you were born near Bosanski Samac; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And when you finished school, you became employed, after some time, in Bosanski Samac; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: What was the date that you moved from Bosanski Samac to Rudine?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In January 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: What was the purpose of your move from Bosanski Samac to the village of Rudine?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I moved mostly because of the job opportunity. I could make much more money working for a private company, and I had some other business in progress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Todorovic, did you receive any threats while in Bosanski Samac? Did you feel under a threat in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Nobody threatened me in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: If that has clarified, Your Honour, the Defence has no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, I think we will take the break now and return at 5 minutes after four, and we will conclude at a quarter to five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, I thought it was Mr. Niemann's turn. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: During the break, I remembered three direct questions that I forgot to ask. By your leave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, at any time, did you learn the identity of the four individuals?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: When you were in the trunk of the automobile, on the other side of the river, did anybody besides the four men touch you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Who, and how?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who, but I felt, through that tape, because a torch lamp was on, somebody had got me by the chin and said, "Yes, that's him."

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Last question: During your conversation with the general, besides what you have testified to earlier, did he say anything else to you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: He said to me, "See? We can do whatever we like."

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, when you met the officer from the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal at 11.00 on the 27th of September, he informed you of your rights; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He told you that a warrant was in existence?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And that an indictment had been issued by the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did he beat you, or threaten you, or do anything improper of that nature?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this the first time that you heard or saw this person?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I take it you weren't surprised to be informed of the existence of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you were put upon the helicopter, you were blindfolded at that stage?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And in fact you were blindfolded for the whole ride, through the period of time that you were on the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, during the whole ride by the helicopter, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you couldn't help us by telling us what -- or to whom the helicopter belonged?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say who it belonged to, but if it landed at the American base in Tuzla, I don't know who else's helicopter could land there. It had to belong to them or somebody who was close to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said in your evidence that you had seen people in SFOR uniforms on a number of occasions prior to September 27th of 1998. Where had you seen these people in SFOR uniforms?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The first I saw them on television, on a television screen, and then I also had an opportunity of seeing them on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where on the road? In what part of the country?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you assist us, is there any particular part in the Republika Srpska that you saw them?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I used to see them between Banja Luka and Bijeljina, somewhere along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you didn't see these people when you were in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, did you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I saw vehicles on one occasion near Zvornik, by the Drina River; but otherwise, no, I did not see them in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you never encountered or met anyone in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia from the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the people that you say captured you from your house in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia spoke in the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And they appeared to be familiar with where they were going? You didn't hear any discussion about directions, or anything of that sort, did you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were not quite sure, not all the time, because meanwhile they were discussing whether to go to the left or to the right, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You don't recall them getting lost, or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that they got lost at any time, but I do know they stopped off and would return in the opposite direction and get off the road and drive back and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the civilian number plate that was on the car that you observed, that was a civilian number plate of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or Serb?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you saw that between the time you were taken from the house to the car?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before they put me into the car. As I was walking toward the car, I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did they put the blindfold over your eyes? At what stage?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: They blindfolded me when they got off the highway between Podgorica and Belgrade, and perhaps after an hour journey, at an elevation where there were neither houses, nor people, nor vehicles. Nobody was passing by, nor were there any inhabited houses nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In answer to a question from His Honour, you said that you left Bosanski Samac in January of 1998. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had you stayed in Bosanski Samac all of the time, from, say, 1992 up until 1998, or had you been in other places, lived in other places?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I lived in Bosanski Samac all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you say one of the reasons that you went to the Federal Republic of Serbia was because of employment opportunities. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you would agree with me, would you not, that you also went there to avoid being arrested by officers of the International Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So that was not a matter that ever entered your head when you moved from Bosanski Samac to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It never occurred to you that it might be advantageous for you to leave Bosnia and move to Serbia in order to avoid being arrested on the indictment that you knew had been issued against you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I knew about the indictment, but that was not the crucial, the decisive reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I didn't ask you whether it was the only reason; I just said it was one of the reasons. You'd agree with me, would you not, that it was one of the reasons why you went there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the money that was to be dropped off, the additional ransom money of 40.000 Deutschmarks, that was to be dropped off, if it was paid, at a gas station outside Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, knowing of the existence of the indictment that had been issued by the Tribunal, why didn't you turn yourself in to the authorities in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Objection. Immaterial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question is allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you answer my question, please?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By all means. Knowing of the existence of the indictment that had been issued by the Tribunal against you, why didn't you turn yourself in to the authorities at either Tuzla or anywhere else in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I hadn't been finished all my private affairs, things that I had to do. Perhaps I would have turned myself in later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, you told us you really wouldn't know whether one of the reasons for you moving to Serbia was to avoid being arrested on this indictment. You knew about it. Why is it that you call Serbia or the Federal Republic a country of refuge?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It was not a refuge. I basically went there to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You understand, don't you, that your application or one of your applications here is to be returned to what is called your country of refuge; that is, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I do not fully understand the term "refuge."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I see. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: May I be heard, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: The term "country of refuge," I don't think my client has even seen the term. I am using it as a term of art which I have purloined from a number of decisions. That is my phrase to explain a legal concept, and not the witness's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Brashich?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. Just a small intervention. Maybe a problem with the term in the Serbian language, in these languages. May I have a suggestion to the interpreters to use the word "izbjeglistvo" instead of "utociste." There is a very tiny difference between these two meanings of the same word. [Interpretation] "Izbjeglistvo," in the sense of a country where one goes when they feel threatened in the country where they come from, either in the sense of human rights or some other reasons. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I would add to Mr. Pantelic's Serbian explanation that a "izbjeglistvo" can also be an economic -- an individual who has moved countries for economic reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, I think you can make submissions later. Do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'd just like to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In answer to Mr. Brashich, you said the General said, "See, we can do whatever we like." At what stage in the proceedings was that said, or was it said in response to any particular comment or observation that you had made?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: General Sinseki [phoen] first asked me what he was to do in order to get to Blagoje Simic, and I said that I didn't know. Then he said, "You see, we can do whatever we want to do, whatever we set out to do."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brashich, you have other evidence, other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: For today, no, Your Honour. As I had reported to the Registry, I have sent out my investigator to contact the two witnesses that I alluded to yesterday, and he was supposed to report back to me today. I probably expect a message or a fax at the hotel advising me of their availability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have the possibility -- and the senior legal advisor can advise me on this -- I think we have the possibility of continuing these proceedings next week, Wednesday and Thursday. At any rate, after the contempt -- after the conclusion of the contempt proceedings. That may take two days. If it runs into a third day, then it would be Thursday that would be available to us. If they are concluded on Tuesday, then Wednesday would be available to us. We would have to advise you as to the precise date when these proceedings would resume, but we would expect at that time, Mr. Brashich, that you would be in a position to call your witnesses, if you have them. Otherwise, I think we'll have to proceed to submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, with regard to the two witnesses, they are short, and knowing the judicial time is short and dear, one of the things which I was contemplating, I did not have a chance to speak to my client about it, but I would tender a stipulation to the Prosecution. Attached to it would be a sworn declaration. I don't think that the issues which these two witnesses will testify to is going to be in any way -- well, that's one of the thoughts that I had. The second thing, Your Honour, if the Court is gracious to leave me some time on Thursday, perhaps in the meantime, if the Court has the time available to address the motion that I filed this morning, because should that evidence be allowed by the Chamber, then I would request a subpoena or a judicial fiat producing the three witnesses that I had requested, the documentary evidence, and the tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, we only just received your motion shortly before this afternoon's proceedings started. We're not in a position to comment on it now. Indeed, I think the Prosecution is entitled to respond to it. We will take the adjournment, and you will be advised as to when the resumption will take place. We'll take the adjournment now.
